title: Social support is unevenly distributed and associated with mental-health burden
source_unit: CDC 2022 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System analysis using the Social Determinants and Health Equity and Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity modules
geography: 26 U.S. states; noninstitutionalized adults aged 18 or older

denominator.unit: analytic-sample adults in 26 states after exclusions

loneliness.unit: percent reporting always, usually, or sometimes feeling socially isolated

lack_of_social_emotional_support.unit: percent reporting sometimes, rarely, or never getting needed social and emotional support

loneliness_income_below_25000.unit: percent weighted prevalence among households below $25,000

loneliness_transgender_range.unit: percent weighted prevalence across reported transgender groups

adjusted_prevalence_ratio_loneness_to_st.unit: adjusted prevalence ratio comparing adults reporting loneliness with those who did not

later_belonging_action_recovery.unit: support received, care use, belonging, civic participation, trust, recovery, and persistence

observations.method: Weighted prevalence estimates and adjusted prevalence ratios from the 2022 BRFSS Social Determinants and Health Equity and Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity modules; social connection and mental-health measures are kept as distinct cross-sectional outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: Only 26 states reported both modules, responses are self-reported, response rates varied, missingness was material for some measures, and the 2022 question measured feeling socially isolated rather than the direct loneliness wording used in 2023.
observations.subgroup: Adults by age, income, race and ethnicity, sex, household structure, sexual orientation, and gender identity; subgroup differences are descriptive and adjusted associations do not establish mechanisms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Loneliness and mental-health measures may share causes, and mental-health difficulty may also shape perceived connection. A higher prevalence ratio is not a causal effect of loneliness, and social contact is not automatically needed support.

boundary: This record adds unequal social-connection prevalence and adjusted cross-sectional associations with mental-health measures. It does not follow the same person through social disruption, support received, care, belonging, trust, civic action, recovery, or persistence, and it does not establish causation.
